newsitem.title: USA: Cuban diplomats brief U.S. Congress staffers.
newsitem.headline: Cuban diplomats brief U.S. Congress staffers.

text.p: Cuban diplomats on Tuesday held a rare public briefing in a U.S. Congress office building, legislative staff members and diplomats said.

Three diplomats from the Cuban interests section in Washington met for over one hour with some 30 staffers and guests for an informal briefing on Cuba sponsored by four prominent Democrats of the Black Caucus.
Staffers and diplomats who attended the meeting said they could recall no such encounter in Congress between officials of the United States and Cuba, which broke diplomatic links over 35 years ago.

"The most important thing is that there is a willingness to dialogue," said one legislative assistant, who asked not to be named. "We heard their point of view, and that is something we don't get to hear too often."

A Cuban diplomat declined to comment on the meeting, but confirmed that interests section deputy chief Felix Wilson and third secretaries Johana Tablada and Sergio Martinez had taken part in the discussion.
The briefing was organised by the offices of Reps. John Conyers of Michigan, Ron Dellums of California, Earl Hilliard of Alabama and Charles Rangel of New York.
The congressmen, who did not attend the meeting as the House of Representatives is in recess, are opposed to the trade embargo Washington has kept on Havana since 1962.
Staffers said the Cubans talked about U.S.-Cuba relations, going back to the early 19th century when the island was still a Spanish colony and some U.S. political leaders called for its annexation.

They also said that despite the U.S. sanctions, Cuba's economy was rebounding from the shock it suffered during the first half of this decade due to the collapse of the Soviet Union, its longtime supporter.
The Cuban diplomats took questions about the human rights situation and the island's political system, staff members said. Cuba is the Western Hemisphere's only communist nation.

Cuban-American legislators frequently complain that the United States gives Cuban diplomats too much liberty to meet scholars, students and business people, arguing that Havana is far more strict with U.S. diplomats in Cuba.
The United States has charged that its diplomats have been harassed in Cuba for meeting with dissidents and human rights activists.
